title: Consistent 2D game assets created by Astra in Blender with GPT Images 2.0 as reference.
author: UnfortunateHurricane
selftext:
Hey,

the game I am working on will include a pizza builder. 

For that I have been looking into how to create assets which are consistent in style.


I created the assets first as reference via GPT Images 2.0. 
And planned on just redrawing them in Inkscape. I only managed to draw my salami slice in inkscape so far and kinda dreaded to continue there. 

To me this approach looks like a viable option. Let me know what you think. Each asset took about 1-2% of pro lite weekly quota.

https://i.imgur.com/z8i0EI5.png

https://i.imgur.com/5rsyE5q.png



This is how astra desrcibes the workflow:


      asset_pipeline/
      ├── shared/
      │   ├── geometry.py       # Mesh creation, curves, bounds, parenting
      │   ├── style.py          # Materials, shading nodes, outline compositor
      │   └── export.py         # Camera, framing, rendering, scene saving
      ├── ingredients/
      │   └── example/
      │       ├── build.py      # Geometry and variants for this ingredient
      │       ├── sheet.py      # PNG checks and comparison-sheet composition
      │       └── render.ps1    # Runs Blender, then regular Python
      └── output/
          ├── ingredient.blend
          ├── inspection/
          ├── pieces/
          └── manifest.json
    
  The reusable modules correspond to our blender_common.py and blender_family.py; each ingredient has its
  own build.py.

  1. Translate the style master into explicit settings.

     A master can be a generated image, painting, sprite or render. Someone first interprets its visual
     treatment and records decisions such as:
    
         {
           "nominal_canvas": [64, 64],
           "export_scale": 4,
           "supersample": 3,
           "outline_px_at_nominal": 1.0,
           "projection": "orthographic_top_down",
           "shading": "two_tone"
         }

     Ingredient palettes define material roles such as skin, flesh and seeds, with a base and shade colour
     for each.

     Passing the style down means importing the same shader and export code into every ingredient builder.
     The master image itself does not have to be embedded in the assets.

  2. Generate actual meshes in the ingredient’s build.py.

     Blender’s Python API accepts vertex coordinates and faces:

         import bpy
    
         mesh = bpy.data.meshes.new("IngredientMesh")
         mesh.from_pydata(vertices, [], faces)
         mesh.update()
    
         obj = bpy.data.objects.new("Ingredient", mesh)
         bpy.context.collection.objects.link(obj)
         obj.data.materials.append(material)
    
         The ingredient-specific work is calculating vertices and faces.
    
         For a ring, define a cross-section containing the outer wall, top surface and inner wall. Sweep each
         cross-section point around an angle:
    
         x = radius * math.cos(angle)
         y = radius * math.sin(angle)
         z = height

     Connect neighbouring samples with quad faces. A full revolution produces a ring; a restricted angular
     range produces a sector, whose ends need closing faces.

     Other forms use different construction methods: extruded outlines for cut pieces, curves with
     thickness for stems, or small flattened meshes for seeds. Bevel and subdivision modifiers soften
     selected edges.

  3. Construct the shared shading system through Python.

     style.py creates a Blender material node group. Our treatment chooses between two colours according
     to a spatial boundary.

     For a generic demonstration, normalize the piece’s projected coordinates to u, v between zero and
     one, then use:

         boundary = 0.35 + 0.30 × (3u² − 2u³)
         colour = shade_colour when v > boundary, otherwise base_colour

     That supplies a simple curved division without revealing a master’s actual path.

     In Blender, this becomes coordinate, math, comparison and colour-mixing nodes feeding an Emission
     shader. Emission gives direct control over flat colours. Our implementation also uses surface
     orientation to shade turned-away sides with the same shade colour.

     Every component belonging to one piece references a shared coordinate Empty. The skin, flesh and
     seeds therefore use one continuous shading boundary.

  4. Build and pose deliberate variants.

     Each ingredient script holds explicit parameters for its variants: thickness, opening size,
     curvature, cut angle, seed placement and orientation.

     The script builds each variant, parents its components to an Empty, applies the pose, then
     establishes its shading coordinates. This ordering keeps the shading aligned consistently when the
     geometry changes orientation.

     Parameters are repeatable. Random variation, if used, should have a recorded seed. Visual corrections
     become changes to those parameters or construction functions.

  5. Generate outlines in the compositor.

     Our outline comes from the rendered silhouette:

     Render alpha
         → expand the mask
         → colour the expanded mask with the outline colour
         → place the original render over it

     In Blender, the relevant nodes are Render Layers, Dilate/Erode, Set Alpha and Alpha Over.

     This makes outline width controllable in render pixels. For the generic configuration above:

     inspection outline = 1 nominal pixel × 4 export scale × 3 supersampling
                        = 12 pixels

     The camera framing must reserve space for this outward expansion.

  6. Render one isolated piece at a time.

     The export script configures the scene:

         scene = bpy.context.scene
         scene.render.engine = "BLENDER_EEVEE"
         scene.render.film_transparent = True
         scene.render.image_settings.file_format = "PNG"
         scene.render.image_settings.color_mode = "RGBA"
         scene.view_settings.view_transform = "Standard"
         camera.data.type = "ORTHO"

     It then hides the other variants, evaluates the current piece’s geometry—including modifiers—and
     calculates its bounds. Those bounds determine the camera centre and orthographic scale.

     For a nominal 64×64 canvas with the example settings:

     nominal canvas:       64 × 64
     exported PNG:        256 × 256
     inspection render:   768 × 768

     Render with bpy.ops.render.render(write_still=True), then downsample. Save the editable scene using
     bpy.ops.wm.save_as_mainfile(...).

  7. Run image checks and compose the review sheets outside Blender.

     Regular Python with Pillow opens the exported PNGs and checks dimensions, transparency, silhouette
     bounds and centering. Ingredient-specific checks can confirm that a ring still has a transparent
     centre.

     The sheet script resizes and places the finished images. It produces both enlarged inspection views
     and a view using explicit placement sizes. A 256-pixel source file might represent a 16-pixel die or
     a 90-pixel ring; that relationship belongs in placement metadata.

     A JSON manifest records variant IDs, dimensions, pivots, intended sizes and source hashes. Automated
     checks establish technical correctness; visual review checks recognition and consistency.

  The launcher connects these stages:

          $blenderExe = 'C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 5.2\blender.exe'
        
          & $blenderExe --background --factory-startup --python-exit-code 1 `
              --python .\ingredients\example\build.py
          if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Blender build failed.' }
        
          python .\ingredients\example\sheet.py
          if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Sheet generation or checks failed.' }

  Blender runs build.py; ordinary Python runs sheet.py. The .blend stores the resulting editable meshes,
  materials and scene. The scripts preserve the construction recipe, so revisions can be regenerated;
  manual edits made only inside the saved scene need transferring back into that recipe to survive a
  rebuild.
